Key inconsistencies/missing items: anti‑desmoglein‑1 and ‑3 ELISAs are documented as "Normal" despite a separate note of "Presence of desmoglein antibodies" (contradiction needing clarification); the histologic level of the split (suprabasal vs subcorneal) is not clearly documented (entries read "Normal"), and mucosal exam/other distribution is not reported. These points are critical to distinguish pemphigus vulgaris from pemphigus foliaceus or rarer seronegative/pustular variants. No medication history to exclude drug‑induced pemphigus. Red flag: contradictory serology entry and lack of explicit suprabasal acantholysis/mucosal status.

REJECT

[FEEDBACK]
The diagnosis of "pemphigus vulgaris" is not definitively supported as documented. To confirm PV (or revise diagnosis), obtain/clarify the following specific items:
- Clarify/resolve serology: provide quantitative anti‑desmoglein‑3 and anti‑desmoglein‑1 ELISA titers (or repeat testing) and reconcile the note "Presence of desmoglein antibodies" with the "Normal" ELISA results.
- Histopathology detail: explicit statement of the level of epidermal split (suprabasal acantholysis with "tombstoning" of basal cells supports PV; subcorneal favors PF).
- Full mucosal examination (oral, conjunctival, genital) and documentation of presence/absence of mucosal lesions.
- Complete medication and medical history to exclude drug‑induced pemphigus and other mimics.
- Consider indirect immunofluorescence/alternative serologic testing if ELISA is negative but clinical/DIF are positive, and consider repeating DIF on perilesional skin if initial sample uncertain.
Optional useful tests: Tzanck smear (acantholytic cells), repeat skin biopsy with more detailed pathology report.

Once these are clarified, a definitive PASS for pemphigus vulgaris can be made if suprabasal acantholysis + DIF intercellular IgG/C3 + positive anti‑Dsg3 (± Dsg1) and mucosal involvement are documented.
